question: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment?

key_points: Continuous Integration: developers frequently merge code into a shared branch, with automated builds/tests running on every merge to catch integration problems early
Continuous Delivery: every change that passes CI is automatically prepared into a release-ready build/artifact, but deployment to production requires a manual trigger/approval
Continuous Deployment: every change that passes all automated checks is automatically deployed straight to production with no manual gate at all
Explains the progression: CI is foundational; delivery and deployment build on top of it, with deployment being the most automated/aggressive end of the spectrum
reference_solution.sample_answer: Continuous Integration means developers frequently merge their code into a shared branch, and automated builds and tests run on every merge to catch integration issues as early as possible, rather than discovering them during a large, infrequent merge. Continuous Delivery builds on that: every change that passes CI is automatically packaged into a release-ready, deployable artifact, but there's still a manual approval or trigger before it actually goes to production. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and removes that manual gate entirely — every change that passes all automated checks is deployed straight to production automatically. So it's a progression: CI is the foundation of frequent integration and automated testing, delivery adds automated release-readiness, and deployment adds full automation all the way to production.

follow_up_hint: Ask what safeguards they'd want in place before trusting continuous deployment with no manual gate at all.

question: What is a blue-green deployment, and how does it reduce deployment risk?

key_points: Two identical production environments ('blue' and 'green') exist; only one serves live traffic at a time
The new version is deployed fully to the idle environment and tested there before any live traffic touches it
Traffic is then switched (via load balancer/router config) from the old environment to the new one, typically nearly instantly
If something's wrong post-switch, rolling back is just switching traffic back to the previous environment — fast and low-risk compared to redeploying the old version
reference_solution.sample_answer: Blue-green deployment maintains two identical production environments, conventionally called blue and green, where only one is actively serving live traffic at any given time. You deploy the new version fully to the currently idle environment and can test it thoroughly there without any risk to live users, since it's receiving no real traffic yet. Once you're confident it's healthy, you switch traffic over — usually by updating the load balancer or router configuration — from the old environment to the new one, which can happen almost instantly. This significantly reduces deployment risk because if something goes wrong after the switch, rolling back is just flipping traffic back to the previous environment, which is fast and doesn't require redeploying or rebuilding the old version from scratch.

follow_up_hint: Ask how blue-green deployment handles database schema migrations that aren't backward-compatible between the two versions.

question: What is a canary deployment, and how does it differ from blue-green deployment?

key_points: Canary deployment gradually rolls out a new version to a small subset of real users/traffic first, monitoring error rates/metrics before progressively increasing the rollout percentage
Blue-green switches ALL traffic at once between two full environments; canary shifts traffic incrementally (e.g. 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%)
Canary catches problems that only manifest under real production traffic/load at a much smaller blast radius than an all-at-once switch

Trade-off: canary is more complex to set up (needs traffic splitting infrastructure and good monitoring/automated rollback triggers) and takes longer to fully roll out than blue-green's instant switch
reference_solution.sample_answer: A canary deployment gradually rolls out a new version to a small percentage of real production traffic first — say 1% — and closely monitors error rates and key metrics before progressively increasing that percentage toward 100% if things look healthy. This differs from blue-green, which switches all traffic from the old environment to the new one essentially at once. Canary's advantage is a much smaller blast radius if something's wrong — only a small fraction of real users are affected before you catch the problem and roll back — whereas blue-green either has everyone on the old version or everyone on the new one. The trade-off is canary requires more sophisticated infrastructure to split traffic by percentage and solid automated monitoring or rollback triggers, and it takes meaningfully longer to complete a full rollout compared to blue-green's essentially instant cutover.

follow_up_hint: Ask what specific metrics they'd monitor to automatically decide whether to proceed with or roll back a canary rollout.

question: Why is it recommended to run automated tests in a CI pipeline before merging code, rather than relying on manual testing alone?

key_points: Automated tests run consistently and quickly on every change, catching regressions immediately rather than relying on a human remembering to manually re-test everything
Manual testing doesn't scale as the codebase grows — testers can't realistically re-verify every existing feature for every small change
Automated tests provide fast feedback directly to the developer who made the change, while context is still fresh, rather than a bug surfacing much later

Doesn't eliminate the need for manual/exploratory testing entirely — automated tests catch known, previously-specified behavior; humans are still valuable for exploratory testing and catching genuinely new classes of issues
reference_solution.sample_answer: Automated tests run consistently and quickly on every single change, catching regressions immediately, without depending on a human remembering to manually re-test every previously working feature — which becomes completely impractical as a codebase and its feature set grow. They also give the developer who made the change fast feedback while the context is still fresh in their mind, rather than a bug being discovered days or weeks later by a manual tester or, worse, a user in production, at which point it's much more expensive to diagnose and fix. That said, automated tests aren't a full replacement for manual testing — they can only catch behavior someone thought to specify in a test case, so exploratory manual testing still has real value for catching genuinely new or unexpected classes of issues automated coverage wouldn't anticipate.

follow_up_hint: Ask what they'd do if the CI test suite became slow enough that developers started skipping or ignoring it.
